title: How do you tell if this problem actually needs a distributed system, or if one strong machine would do?
summary: A senior-signal gut-check — tests whether estimation is used to avoid over-building, not just to justify scale, by checking the numbers against what a single modern machine can actually handle.

slides.markdown:
Most candidates reach for a distributed architecture by reflex, because that's what a system-design interview seems to reward. This question checks the opposite instinct: can you use your own estimates to argue that a single strong machine is genuinely enough, when the numbers say so?

Modern hardware is bigger than most candidates assume — hundreds of gigabytes of RAM, dozens of cores, fast NVMe disks — and a real chunk of "system design" problems fit comfortably on one well-tuned box.

Ask: **what's the actual peak QPS and data size right now** — not the eventual, aspirational scale the product might reach in five years if everything goes well. Designing for today's real numbers, with a documented plan for what changes later, is a stronger answer than pre-building for a hypothetical scale that may never arrive.

Many interview prompts drift toward "but what if this becomes huge" — it's fine to note that as a future consideration, but the sizing decision itself should be grounded in the numbers actually given.

The method: **compare the estimate against a single high-end machine's known capacity** — RAM, cores, disk IOPS — **before** reaching for a cluster. A modern high-memory instance can offer 256GB-1TB of RAM, dozens of cores, and NVMe disks pushing hundreds of thousands of IOPS; many workloads' real numbers fit comfortably inside that envelope.

See [back-of-envelope fundamentals](back-of-envelope-fundamentals) for the broader estimation habits this check builds on. Say the comparison out loud rather than assuming distribution is required by default.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a workload that fits on one machine
slides.markdown:
A product catalog service: 200GB of data, and a peak load estimated at 30,000 QPS, mostly reads.

```
200 GB data vs 256 GB RAM available -> fits with ~22% headroom
30,000 peak QPS vs ~50,000 QPS a well-tuned single instance can serve for this read-heavy workload
```

Both numbers fit comfortably within a single machine's real capacity — **no cluster is needed yet**. The strong answer says this plainly instead of defaulting to a distributed design the numbers don't actually require.

slides.sectionTitle: Where a single machine genuinely stops being enough
slides.markdown:
The limit isn't only raw capacity — it's also **durability**. Even a machine with capacity to spare is still one box: a single disk failure, a single power event, takes the entire service down with it. That's a real constraint the moment availability matters, independent of whether the numbers say the machine has headroom left.

Say this distinction explicitly: "the numbers say one machine can handle the load, but if this needs to survive a machine failure, that's a separate requirement capacity math alone doesn't satisfy."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: checking whether the workload is CPU-, memory-, or I/O-bound
slides.markdown:
A single machine's real ceiling depends entirely on which resource the workload actually exhausts first:

```
I/O-bound (waiting on network/disk):   ~50,000 QPS is realistic
CPU-bound (heavy per-request compute):  ~5,000-10,000 QPS, even with ample RAM
Memory-bound (working set > RAM):       throughput drops sharply once cache misses dominate
```

The 50,000 QPS figure from the earlier example assumed an I/O-bound workload — the same machine running a CPU-bound version of the same feature could be an order of magnitude short of that ceiling, so naming which category applies is not optional detail, it's the number that decides the whole answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a single machine's simplicity vs being a single point of failure
slides.markdown:
**A single machine** is simpler to build, operate, and reason about — no distributed consistency, no cross-node coordination, no partition tolerance to design around. **A distributed setup** costs real complexity up front, but removes the single point of failure the moment one machine dying would be unacceptable.

The trade isn't capacity vs no capacity — it's simplicity vs survivability, and the right call depends entirely on whether the prompt requires surviving a node failure, not on the QPS or data-size numbers alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "assume this must survive a machine failure"
slides.markdown:
If the interviewer adds that constraint, the answer changes even though the QPS and data-size numbers didn't. At minimum, that means at least one standby replica of the machine's data and a way to fail over to it — the simplest fix is a hot standby rather than a full horizontal cluster, since capacity was never the problem, only durability was.

Saying "the capacity math didn't force this, but the failure requirement does" shows you understand these are two separate reasons to distribute, not one blended justification.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: build for a distributed future now, or later?
slides.markdown:
"Your estimate says one machine is enough today — do you still design for a distributed future, or build it when you need it?" The strong middle ground: keep the app **stateless** and the data-access layer behind an interface, so migrating to a distributed data tier later is a swap, not a rewrite — without actually building or operating that distributed system before the numbers demand it.

Paying the full complexity cost of distribution today, for a scale that may or may not arrive, is the over-engineering this whole question is checking against.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for distributed by default
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** propose a distributed, sharded, multi-region architecture because "that's what system design interviews want to hear."

**Why it's wrong:** it skips the actual estimation the interview is testing for, and it often signals the opposite of seniority — real engineers pay for complexity only when the numbers, or an explicit requirement like durability, actually demand it. Unjustified distribution also invites the interviewer to ask "why not just one machine?" — a question the candidate now has no numeric answer for.

**Correct model:** run the single-machine capacity check first, every time, and only distribute when a specific number or requirement fails it.

Compressed script: "At 200GB of data and 30,000 peak QPS, both fit comfortably within a single high-end machine's real capacity — 256GB of RAM and roughly 50,000 QPS for this I/O-bound workload. I wouldn't distribute based on capacity alone. If this needs to survive a machine failure, that's a separate, durability-driven reason to add a standby, not a capacity-driven one."

Practice actually saying "one machine is enough" out loud when the numbers support it — resisting the reflex to over-build is the actual signal here.
